issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient also directly sustained major physical injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of medical cues can fit some trauma-to-a-loved-one cases, but in this profile it appears to be driven by a personal bodily injury/medical trauma theme that is otherwise unsupported except by the implausible physical-vulnerability appraisal, making this item clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Sister Mary had been a nun for over 30 years. Known for her dedication to her faith and her community, she was always seen as someone who could provide comfort and guidance to those around her. However, everything changed one fateful day when tragedy struck. It was an unusually quiet Sunday morning at the convent where Sister Mary lived and worked. She had just finished a service and was heading back to her room to prepare for her next task. As she walked through the corridors, a phone call came from one of the sisters who had gone out to visit family. The news was devastating: her brother, who had been visiting his home town, had died in a car accident. The impact of this loss was immediate and profound. Sister Mary found herself struggling with a flood of memories that would come without warning, triggered by something as simple as the sound of tires rolling on wet pavement or even the scent of incense from the church. The memory of her brother's death was vividly detailed in some moments-she could see his car spinning out of control, hear the screeching of brakes-but other details remained entirely blank. Sister Mary had come to believe that she should have protected him somehow, and this belief fueled her intense self-blame. She couldn't shake the thought that if only she had insisted on speaking with him one last time or made sure he took a different route home, perhaps things would have turned out differently. This constant self-criticism had eroded her confidence in herself, making it difficult for her to trust her own judgment and abilities. In an attempt to cope with these overwhelming memories and feelings of guilt, Sister Mary developed several maladaptive strategies. She began avoiding the area where the accident occurred, even if it meant taking a longer route when traveling. Any mention or reminder of her brother would trigger intense grief and anxiety, so she actively avoided such triggers. This avoidance included not only physical reminders but also mental ones-she performed intricate mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again. Over time, these behaviors began to take a toll on Sister Mary's life. She found herself isolating more often, preferring the solitude of her room where she could control her environment and avoid triggers. This isolation strained her relationships with other sisters at the convent, who noticed her withdrawal but didn't understand why it was happening. What frightened her most was the fear that these memories would never fade and that she would continue to blame herself for something out of her control. The nagging doubt about her ability to protect others had made her second-guess every decision she made, leading her to feel increasingly helpless and ineffective in her role as a nun. It wasn't until Sister Mary found herself unable to attend the funeral of another loved one due to an overwhelming sense of dread that she realized she needed help. The thought of reliving those painful memories and facing her fears alone was too much to bear. She finally decided to seek therapy, hoping to find ways to manage these intrusive thoughts and regain a sense of control over her life. In therapy, Sister Mary expressed her deepest hopes for recovery: to be able to remember her brother without feeling overwhelmed by guilt and to regain the confidence in herself that she once had. She was determined to break free from the grip of these memories and avoidances so she could return to being the compassionate and strong presence she once was at the convent.
